transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-21 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Chandra (Redwood SE), Daniel Wu (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (MeridianMesh - Head of Cloud Partnerships), Tom Erickson (Infra Lead), Rina Patel (PM), Jae Kim (Security)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. This is Alex from Redwood, AE, and with me is Priya and Daniel, our SEs. How's everyone doing at MeridianMesh?
[00:06] Sofia: Hi Alex, doing well. Quick intro: I'm Sofia, I lead cloud partnerships. Tom and Rina are on the infra and product side, and Jae is our security architect. Thanks for doing this.
[00:14] Alex: Great. The goal today is high level partner framing — understand your onramp needs for GPU capacity, what integration points matter, compliance blockers, and what a good pilot looks like. We'll leave time at the end for Qs. Sound good?
[00:26] Tom: Sounds good. We're mainly exploring a channel integration where MeridianMesh customers can route workloads to Redwood-driven inference. Two modes we're considering: a fully hosted lane and a co-managed private onramp where we peer into customer VPCs.
[00:38] Priya: Nice. Can you say more about typical workloads and latency/cost expectations? Even ballparks help.
[00:44] Rina: Most of our customers run large batching text-generation for internal search and conversational assistants. Peak RPS is relatively low per-customer but aggregated could be hundreds of concurrent streams. Latency SLOs differ: interactive flows want <200ms tail, batch can be seconds. Cost sensitivity is high — they care about per-token unit economics.
[01:05] Daniel: Understood. On the Redwood side we have three deployment modes: hosted API, Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). For a channel integration you can route by policy; for private onramp we usually do VPC peering or a customer-managed private control plane depending on regs.
[01:21] Jae: On security, we need to validate SSO/SSAML flows, KMS/HSM integration for key custody, and audit logging. We prefer not to send unencrypted user data to third-party hosts. SOC2 is a minimum.
[01:31] Alex: Totally. We can share our SOC2 summary and our KMS options — we support both customer-managed KMS via HSM-backed providers and Redwood-managed keys with strict audit logs. We'll annotate where logs are stored and what gets redacted.
[01:42] Sofia: A couple quick clarifying Qs: 1) how does routing work when you have Dedicated pools vs hosted? 2) what's the fallback behavior if capacity is constrained?
[01:49] Priya: For routing we can policy-match by customer tier, latency SLO, cost bucket, or region. If dedicated pool is full we can fall back to a cheaper hosted variant or a smaller-quantized model; fallback is configurable with canary thresholds. Sometimes the transcriber says 'fall back to cheap' — sorry, I mean 'cheaper model variant'.
[02:09] Tom: How intrusive is VPC peering — do we have to open ports or run agents? We have strict firewall posture.
[02:15] Daniel: There are a few patterns. 1) VPC peering with strict ACLs and Egress rules, 2) VPC PrivateLink-style endpoints, or 3) on-prem appliance for air-gapped. Each has tradeoffs. PrivateLink avoids wide-open peering but needs endpoint setup. We can provide Terraform templates.
[02:30] Rina: Perf testing — we want to benchmark a typical 2k token generation with a 4k context. Are there known perf profiles for that?
[02:37] Priya: We have perf profiles per model; for long context workloads we pick kernels and kv cache strategies. We'll run a baseline but note quantization will change throughput. We'll likely recommend int8 or q4 mixed depending on model arch. Also mention — transcription sometimes munges 'q4' as 'queue for' — but we really talk about quantization levels.
[02:56] Sofia: On commercials, MeridianMesh is leaning toward an initial pilot that we co-sell. We need predictable pricing — reserved capacity looks appealing, but we also need burst for spikes.
[03:05] Alex: For pilots we do a hybrid: reserved for baseline throughput + burst on hosted. We can model costs in a spreadsheet — we'll share a sample TCO comparing reserved vs pure hosted.
[03:14] Jae: Can you describe what audit logs include? We need per-request token usage, redaction markers, and model version used. Also how long logs are retained.
[03:22] Daniel: Logs include metadata (request id, model id/version, latency, token counts), and optional payloads if you enable them. Retention is configurable; enterprise plans let you push logs to your SIEM or S3 for long-term retention. We can redact PII at ingest with configurable rules.
[03:36] Tom: Network egress charges — if we peer, who pays for egress between MeridianMesh and Redwood infra?
[03:42] Priya: Usually the party hosting infra covers their cloud egress. For Dedicated deployments on your region we can host within your account to avoid cross-account egress, or we can co-locate. We'll pull cost assumptions into the TCO.
[03:54] Sofia: Any constraints around model pinning and rollouts? Some customers require strict model pinning for reproducibility.
[04:01] Alex: Yes — customers can pin model versions and pin config. Rollouts support canary and A/B with automatic fallback. We also keep model provenance metadata for audits.
[04:10] Rina: Integration surface — do you expose an SDK or only REST?
[04:14] Daniel: We have REST and SDKs across major languages. For partners we can surface a partner SDK that handles auth and routing policies so you can route to Redwood without exposing raw keys to end customers.
[04:27] (background: brief cross talk)
[04:32] Priya: Quick risk note: quantized models sometimes have small accuracy regressions. We'll recommend a quality guardrail test set. Redwood Optimize helps with suggestions and monitors regressions.
[04:45] Sofia: Good. Thinking about next steps — we'd like a short pilot with 3 customers, a perf run, and a security review. Is that feasible in 4 weeks?
[04:53] Alex: Yes — pilot kickoff in 3-4 weeks is feasible. Priya can run perf baselines asap. We'll need your SOC2 and sample workload.
[04:59] Jae: On SOC2 — we may have additional cross-border data residency rules. Are there region restrictions?
[05:05] Daniel: We support region pinning and can route to hosted regions in NA/EU/APAC. For stricter residency we'll recommend Redwood Private deployed in your region or dedicated within your cloud project.
[05:15] Tom: A technical deep dive question: how do you handle KV cache eviction across shards? We saw ‘K V cache’ become a meme in the notes.
[05:22] Priya: We do sharded KV per GPU and Azure — sorry, per-gpu/gpu-node. Eviction policy is LRU-ish and we do prefix caching to reduce warm-start. For cross-shard coordination we avoid synchronous locks by routing prefixes to the same shard when possible. There's some heuristics there.
[05:39] Rina: Is there an onboarding flow for partners to get credentials and scopes so they can call the partner API on behalf of customers?
[05:46] Alex: Yes, partner tokens and scoped keys — we support OAuth flows for delegated access and token scoping. We'll provide an integration checklist.
[05:55] Sofia: Can you share any references or partner decks?
[05:58] Alex: We'll share our partner deck and an integration checklist (Drive link) after the call. Also a sample SOW template for pilots.
[06:07] (long silence while speakers scan)
[06:20] Tom: Cost sensitivity aside, what are common pitfalls you've seen with channel onramps?
[06:25] Daniel: Three big ones: 1) underestimating request pattern spikiness — lead to token queuing, 2) not accounting for KV warm-up costs on cold starts, 3) insufficient monitoring on quality regressions after quantization or model swaps. We help with tooling but it's common.
[06:44] Rina: For our pilots we'd like to test one LLM-heavy flow and one embedding use case. Is embedding routing different?
[06:51] Priya: Embeddings are usually lower-latency but high QPS. We recommend dedicated CPU/accelerator pools or batched embedding pools. Caching helps a lot for repeated content.
[07:05] Jae: A security nit: do you support bringing-your-own-HSM for key custody?
[07:10] Daniel: Yes, BYO-KMS/HSM is supported in Redwood Private or Dedicated when we federate keys. We'll map the key lifecycle and access policies in the SOC2 appendix.
[07:20] Sofia: Great. Anything else on the architectural side?
[07:24] Priya: For route policy we can set a 'cost cap' so queries exceeding spend thresholds fall back. Also canary rollouts if a new model underperforms.
[07:33] Tom: If we were to run a 2-week pilot, what success metrics do you recommend?
[07:38] Alex: 1) latency tail (95/99) below agreed SLOs, 2) per-token cost vs target TCO, 3) qualitative correctness from a small eval prompt set, 4) integration operational readiness (tokens, keys, logs).
[07:51] Sofia: Who from Redwood will own the pilot?
[07:54] Alex: I'll own commercial and scoping; Priya/Daniel will own tech/run perf. We'll put them down as SE owners.
[08:02] (short pause)
[08:05] Rina: On the legal/commercial side, what's typical contract length for Dedicated reserved capacity?
[08:10] Alex: Dedicated often comes with 12–36 month commits. For pilots we do month-to-month or short trial credits and then a migration path to reserved. Pricing tiers depend on GPU type and SLA.
[08:22] Jae: For auditability, we will need a signed DPA and clarity around data flows prior to pilot.
[08:29] Alex: Absolutely. We'll loop legal and send a draft DPA and the SSO flow.
[08:34] Sofia: Anything else from MeridianMesh?
[08:36] Tom: Quick ops concern — do you support autoscaling policies tied to queue length or token-per-second thresholds?
[08:43] Priya: Yes. Autoscaling is policy-driven — we support queue-length, CPU/GPU utilization, and token throughput as triggers. There's also burst policies for short spikes.
[08:55] Sofia: OK let's outline immediate outcomes: 1) Redwood sends integration checklist + partner deck, 2) MeridianMesh shares SOC2 excerpt + sample workload, 3) SE perf baseline. Agree?
[09:06] All: Agree.
[09:09] (noise, shuffling)
[09:15] Alex: We'll put these as action items in the follow up and send calendar invites for the perf window and technical deep dive.
[09:22] Sofia: Great, thanks everyone.
[09:25] Alex: Thank you all. We'll follow up with links.

Notes on transcription: some proper nouns may be slightly off; 'KV' often transcribed as 'K V', 'quantization' occasionally as 'queue nization' and 'Redwood Dedicated' as 'Redwood Dedicatede' in auto captions.

Call end: 16:52 UTC

Recap (short): Pilot framed for 3 customers, baseline perf run to be run by Redwood SEs, security artifacts to be exchanged. Next big milestone: perf baseline results and technical deep dive scheduled next week.
